readerTitle: Dana's app needs six weeks to get smart. What do you give away?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (작은 동네 상점용 재고·발주 앱 ShelfSense) · 고객은 소매점, 제품은 소프트웨어 · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 무료 등급과 무료 체험은 둘 중 하나를 고르는 문제가 아니다. 고객이 가치를 처음 느끼는 시점과 무료 고객 한 명을 유지하는 비용에 맞춰, 무엇을 영원히 주고 무엇을 잠깐 맛보게 할지 설계하는 문제다.
misconception: 무료 등급은 관대하고 무료 체험은 효율적이니 둘 중 하나만 고르면 된다. 체험 기간은 업계 관행대로 14일이면 충분하다.

sources.text: 모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 사례
무료 등급(freemium)과 무료 체험(free trial)의 일반적인 구분, 가치 도달 시간(time to value) 개념

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 3번째 결정 계산: 가입 2,000곳 중 유료 80곳(4%), 무료 1,920곳 × 월 $1 = 월 $1,920, 유료 매출 80 × $30 = 월 $2,400. 카드에는 비용 '약 $1,920'만 적었습니다.
'예측이 쓸 만해지려면 판매 기록 약 6주가 필요하다'는 이야기 속 가정입니다. 실제 수요 예측 도구의 필요 데이터 기간으로 일반화하지 않도록 문구를 유지하세요.
각 결정을 유닛 개념(무료 모델, 무료 플랜 vs 체험, 사용량 기반 가격, 락인)에 연결한 정리가 형제 레슨 BMO-03-02, 03-05, 03-06, 03-08의 정의와 어긋나지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Dana's app needs six weeks to get smart.
body: Dana built ShelfSense, an app for small independent shops: corner stores, hardware stores, gift shops. Owners scan deliveries and sales into it.
After about six weeks of sales history, it starts telling them what to reorder and when. But most shop owners decide whether a tool is worth it within days.
Over the next four decisions, you run Dana's launch.

image.label: A corner shop owner scanning shelves with a phone, a calendar marked at week six
image.brief: 따뜻한 조명의 작은 동네 상점 카운터. 주인이 휴대폰으로 선반 상품을 스캔하고 있고, 뒤쪽 벽 달력의 '6주 차'에 동그라미. 휴대폰 화면은 단순한 재고 목록. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표가 보이는 상품은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What do you give away?
body: ShelfSense has two parts. **Stock counting** is useful from day one and cheap to run. **Reorder predictions** are what shops would pay for, at $30 a month per store, but they need six weeks of data.

options.text: A 14-day free trial of everything, then $30 a month
options.feedback: The trial ends on day 14. Predictions start around week six. Most shops leave having seen only a stock counter.

options.text: Everything free forever, and figure out money later
options.feedback: Sign-ups come fast, but you've given away the part people would pay for. Every shop adds server cost with no path to revenue.

options.text: Stock counting free forever, predictions paid
options.feedback: The free part is useful on its own and cheap to serve. Every week a shop uses it, it builds the data the paid part needs.

cards.title: Say you chose the free tier. Now what?
body: Six weeks in, hundreds of shops have enough sales history. None has seen a prediction yet.
How do they find out predictions are worth $30?

options.text: Show a locked "Upgrade to see predictions" button
options.feedback: Clear and cheap to build. But you're asking shops to pay for something they've never seen work on their own shelves.

options.text: Once a shop has six weeks of data, unlock predictions free for 30 days
options.feedback: The trial starts when the product can prove itself. Owners see real reorder advice for their own stock, then decide.

options.text: Give every new shop a 30-day prediction trial on sign-up day
options.feedback: Same trial, wrong clock. It runs out two weeks before the data is ready.

cards.title: Say you timed the trial to the data. A year passes.
body: 2,000 shops have signed up and 80 pay. Free shops cost about $1 each a month to serve, roughly $1,920 in total. Most of that comes from about 150 free accounts that run several locations.
An investor says: drop the free tier.

options.text: Drop the free tier and offer only trials
options.feedback: You cut the bill, but also the stream of shops building data. Next year's paying customers are this year's free ones.

options.text: Keep it free for one location; a second store needs the paid plan
options.feedback: Multi-store owners get the most value and cost the most. The price now follows use, and small shops stay in the pipeline.

options.text: Keep everything free and add supplier ads to the stock screen
options.feedback: It may cover the bill. But supplier ads next to the stock list make owners wonder whose side the app is on.

cards.title: Say you drew the line at one store. Someone wants to leave.
body: A free-tier hardware store wants to try a rival app. The owner asks for a copy of 18 months of sales history.

options.text: Refuse. The data lives in ShelfSense
options.feedback: It might keep this one shop. It also tells every owner that signing up means getting stuck, and neighboring shop owners talk.

options.text: Allow it, for a $50 export fee
options.feedback: Less hostile than refusing, but it still feels like a toll on leaving. And the fee won't move your revenue.
Your real hold is the habit and predictions that already work. Owners who know they can leave trust you enough to stay.

cards.title: Free tier or free trial: two different clocks
body: A **free tier** gives part of the product away forever. It works when the free part is useful alone, cheap to serve, and leads toward the paid part. A **free trial** gives the whole product for a short time. It works when value shows up fast.
So the real questions are when a customer first sees the value, and what one free customer costs you. Dana used both: a tier to build the data, then a trial once the product could prove itself.

image.label: Timeline: free stock counting from day one, prediction trial starting at week six
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 인포그래픽. 0주부터 끝까지 이어지는 연한 띠 "Free tier: stock counting". 6주 차에서 시작하는 진한 30일 구간 "Trial: predictions", 그 뒤 "Paid". 아래에 점선으로 잘못된 14일 체험 구간을 0주에 표시하고 "Ends before value appears" 라벨.

cards.title: Free has to lead somewhere.
body: A free tier only works if a real share of free customers eventually needs the paid part. If the free part does the whole job, most never upgrade.
Free customers also cost money: support, servers and your attention. Track how many upgrade, and what each free one costs, before deciding the tier works.
A shop counter shows the same logic. One free sample of cheese is a trial. A free coffee with every visit is a tier, and it needs a reason to buy something else.

cards.title: Match what's free to when value appears.
body: Each of your four decisions used an idea from this unit:
list: **What to give away** → Free as a model: the free part should build toward the paid part
**When to start the trial** → Free plan or free trial: start the clock when value can show
**Where to draw the line** → Pay-per-use: let the price follow how much a customer uses
**Letting customers leave** → Lock-in: earn it with value, not trapped data
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write down how many days it takes a new customer to first see what you're best at. Does anything you give away free end before that day?
